title: What a Support Group Facilitator Actually Does
summary: Not sure what the job really involves? The work of running a group week to week, from preparing to holding the room to staying well yourself.
body_markdown:
From the outside, facilitating a support group looks like showing up and asking a few questions. The people who do it will tell you the visible ninety minutes are perhaps a third of the work, and the easiest third.


This is what the job actually consists of: before the session, during it, after it, and the part nobody warns you about.


## What the role is, and what it is not


A facilitator holds the structure of a group so that the members can support each other. That is the whole definition, and every specific task follows from it.


The role is not to be the expert who answers questions, the therapist who treats people, or the person who solves the problem in the room. Every one of those is a drift that feels helpful in the moment and weakens the group.


In most of the United States you do not need a license to facilitate a support group, because a support group is not clinical treatment. You do need to stay out of diagnosis and treatment planning, and to avoid protected titles such as therapist, counselor, psychologist or social worker unless you hold that license.


MentalHappy groups are expert-led psychoeducational support groups, supplemental to professional care. Facilitating one is not practicing therapy, and nothing a facilitator does is treatment.


## Before the session


- **The reminder.** Two lines and the joining details, a day ahead. This single habit moves attendance more than anything else a facilitator does.
- **Deciding the shape.** Not a script: a rough plan for the opening, one thing you might raise, and how you will close.
- **Reading the room in advance.** Who said something difficult last week? Who has missed two sessions? A short private message before the session often brings someone back.
- **Admin.** New members, the link, access, anyone who has asked to join. Fifteen unglamorous minutes.
- **Your own state.** Five minutes before you open the room, deliberately, doing nothing. Facilitators who go straight from work into a session facilitate worse and know it.


Total: thirty to forty-five minutes a week for a group that is running smoothly. More when it is not.


## During the session


### Opening


Arrive before everyone, greet people by name, and start on time. Starting late teaches the group that the start time is approximate, and the arrival ritual is more of the work than it looks.


### The check-in


Go round in order, one word or one sentence each. It gets every voice into the room in the first five minutes, which makes speaking later dramatically easier. Go first, and use a real word.


### Holding the middle


This is the actual craft, and it is mostly four moves.


- **Waiting.** Count to ten after a question. More often than not someone speaks, and what they say after a real pause is better.
- **Redirecting.** Acknowledge, summarize, hand on: *That is a lot to be carrying. Has anyone else been sitting with something like that this week?*
- **Protecting.** Someone gives advice that was not asked for, or minimizes what another member said. You name the ground rule, lightly, and move on.
- **Not solving.** The strongest pull in the room is toward fixing. Resisting it, including in yourself, is most of the job.


### Closing


Same form each session, in the same order. Confirm the next date before anyone leaves. If someone said something heavy, do not let them leave without a word. A private line afterward is often the most important thirty seconds of the session.


## After the session


- **Following up.** Anyone who was distressed, anyone who was absent again, anyone who asked for something.
- **A note to yourself.** Three lines: what worked, what did not, what to watch. Not records about members, notes about the group.
- **Putting it down.** The part people skip. Twenty minutes with a co-facilitator, a supervisor or a peer, saying what you carried out of the room.


That last item is not self-indulgence. Facilitators who have nowhere to take what they absorb are the ones who disappear after eight months, and they rarely see it coming.


## The part nobody warns you about


### You will be the only one who knows everything


Members share with the group. They also tell you things privately, before and after, that nobody else hears. Over a year, you accumulate the full picture of eight people's situations and have nobody to discuss it with. This is a specific and under-described load.


### Your own experience will come up


If you are running a group about something you have lived, some week someone will describe your worst month back to you. Deciding in advance how much you share, and being consistent about it, is easier than deciding in the moment.


### People will leave


Sometimes because the group worked and they do not need it any more. That is a success and it will not feel like one.


### You cannot fix it


Members will be in situations that will not improve. The instinct to do something is strong and largely futile, and learning that presence without resolution is the actual offer is the hardest adjustment in the role.


## How many hours is it, really?


Task Per week


Preparation and reminders 30–45 min


The session 60–90 min


Follow-up and notes 20–30 min


Your own debrief 20 min


Recruitment and admin (averaged) 30 min


Roughly three to four hours a week for one group. Planning for ninety minutes and finding it is four is a common reason people stop.


If you are running more than one group, the marginal cost of the second is lower than the first, but the emotional load is not, and that is the constraint that actually binds.


## What good looks like


Not a facilitator who talks a lot, or one with the best questions. The signs a group is being facilitated well are mostly signs of the facilitator's absence:


- Members speak to each other rather than through you.
- Someone has disagreed with someone, and it was fine.
- A member asks how last week's thing went.
- Newer members get helped by slightly older ones without prompting.
- People come back past session four.


If all five are true, you are doing the job, whatever it felt like on the night.


## Questions about the role


### What does a support group facilitator do?


A facilitator holds the structure of the group so that members can support each other: sending reminders, opening and closing consistently, running the check-in, keeping time, protecting the ground rules, and referring on when something exceeds what a support group can hold. They do not assess, diagnose or treat anyone.


### Do I need a qualification to be a support group facilitator?


In most of the United States, no. Facilitating a psychoeducational support group is not a licensed activity because it is not clinical treatment. Training is optional and useful. What is required is staying out of diagnosis and treatment and avoiding protected titles unless you hold that license.


### How many hours a week does running a support group take?


About three to four hours for one group: roughly 30–45 minutes of preparation and reminders, the 60–90 minute session itself, 20–30 minutes of follow-up, and a short debrief for yourself. Most people plan for the session only and are surprised by the rest.


### What is the hardest part of facilitating a support group?


Two things. Resisting the pull to solve people's problems, which feels helpful and weakens the group. And carrying what you absorb, particularly if the subject is close to your own experience, which is why having somewhere to put it is not optional.
